meta_description: This camera permissions guide shows you how to select which apps can access your webcam on Windows, iPhone, Android and in browser privacy settings, and when to revoke it.
h1: Camera Permissions Guide: Turn On Camera Access Safely
subtitle: This camera permissions guide auto-selects your platform and browser to walk you through allowing or resetting camera and microphone access.

How to Tell If Permission Is Already Granted

Each OS shows an indicator whenever the camera is actively in use — check it before assuming permission is the problem

WindowsGreen LED lights whenever any app uses the camera. Check Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera for which apps have permission.
macOSGreen LED next to the camera lights whenever it's active. Check System Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera.
AndroidA green dot appears in the status bar when the camera or mic is active. Check Settings → Privacy → Permission manager → Camera.
iOSA green (camera) or orange (mic) dot appears at the top of the screen. Check Settings → Privacy & Security → Camera.

Want to check right now, on this device, whether something is already holding your camera? Use the Camera In-Use Privacy Check.

content_html:
Every camera on your phone, laptop or tablet sits behind a switch you control, and this camera permissions guide shows you where that switch lives on each operating system. You'll learn how a camera permission is granted, how to review individual apps, and how to keep only the apps you trust able to look through your device's lens.

How Camera Permission Works

A camera permission is a gate, not a camera feature. When an app or site asks to switch the lens on, the system on your device checks three things: your user choice, any stored approval from last time, and the platform policy set by the maker or your employer. Most systems ask on first use and then remember your answer, so the permission state you set once keeps applying until you change it.

That matters because the camera is a live sensor. An app that holds access can watch in real time, not just save photos, so your consent should be a deliberate decision rather than a reflex tap.

The Camera Among Other App Permissions

The camera is one of several permissions your phone or computer tracks for each app. The common ones are:

  • Camera – takes photos, records video and runs video calls
  • Microphone – records sound
  • Location – reads where you are
  • Contacts, calendar and storage – read your personal data
  • Notifications – lets the app send you alerts
  • Bluetooth – connects to nearby accessories

Camera requests often arrive bundled with these, so allow the lens only when your current feature needs it.

Turn On Camera Access in Windows 11 and Windows 10

Windows splits control into one device-wide switch and a set of per-app switches. To find them:

  1. Select Start > Settings > Privacy & security > Camera. On Windows 10 the path is Settings > Privacy > Camera.
  2. Turn Camera access on. This is the device-level switch.
  3. Turn on Let apps access your camera, then switch each listed app on or off.
  4. Turn on Let desktop apps access your camera if programs outside the Store need the lens.

If the camera access setting is greyed out, an administrator controls it, and only they can change it.

Desktop Apps vs Microsoft Store Apps

The per-app list only shows Microsoft Store apps. Programs you installed from the web or a USB drive, or that IT pushed to your machine, count as desktop apps and share a single switch – you can't allow one and block another. Internet browsers such as Microsoft Edge and video conferencing apps such as Microsoft Teams fall in this group, so if a Teams call shows a black preview, check that switch first.

Windows Hello and the Camera App Exceptions

Windows Hello face sign-in keeps working with the camera switch off, because that biometric login sits outside the normal app rules. Some apps also borrow the built-in Camera app to take a photo – they never appear in the list, and they receive nothing until you press the capture button yourself.

Camera and Other Hardware Features on iPhone and iPad

Apple requires every app to ask before it touches the camera and to explain why – a social networking app, for example, has to say it wants the lens so you can post photos. The same rule covers other hardware features such as Bluetooth, the local network and motion and fitness sensors.

  1. Open the Settings app.
  2. Go to Privacy & Security and tap the permission category called Camera.
  3. Use the toggle next to each app to switch its access on or off.

Individual Apps and the Green Indicator

You can also work app by app: scroll down in Settings, tap an app's name and adjust each switch it shows. Whenever the camera is live, a green indicator dot appears at the top of the screen; an orange indicator means the microphone alone is in use. Open Control Center to see which app used either one most recently.

Android App Permissions and the Permission Manager

Android gives you two routes to the same switches. App by app:

  1. Open Settings and tap Apps (tap See all apps if yours isn't listed).
  2. Pick the app and tap Permissions.
  3. Tap Camera and choose to allow or deny access.

Or by permission type: go to Settings > Privacy > Permission manager, tap Camera and review every app that asked for it. Newer phones offer Only while using the app, the safest choice for most application permissions.

Webcam Access in Your Browser Settings

Websites never get the camera directly. The first time a page such as a video call or webcam test wants it, you see a browser prompt asking you to allow or block – and Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari all remember that answer per site.

  • Chrome and Edge: click the site-info icon left of the address bar and set Camera to Allow.
  • Firefox: click the camera icon in the address bar to clear a saved choice.
  • Safari on Mac: open Safari > Settings > Websites > Camera.

If the camera access settings for a site say allowed but the image stays black, the system switch from the sections above is still off – a site-level choice can't override it. Also check any extensions and plug-ins you've given camera rights.

Why Camera Privacy Settings Matter for Security

Camera rights protect against more than spying. An app that keeps access can record faces, a whiteboard or a screen in view, and turn the lens into quiet surveillance inside your normal day. In cybersecurity terms, every approval moves your trust boundary outward to include that app and anything it bundles.

Most trouble comes from overbroad grants ("allow always" for a one-off task), stale approvals on apps you stopped using, and background services or helpers that inherit access from the main program. Treat each live approval as part of your endpoint security, not just a personal preference.

Permission Hygiene: A Camera Permissions Guide Checklist

Good permission hygiene follows least privilege: give camera rights only to trusted services with a current need, and keep every grant revocable. Use this table to find the controls on each platform.

PlatformWhere the setting livesPer-app controlLive indicator
WindowsSettings, Camera pageStore apps only; desktop programs share one switchCamera light on most laptops
iOS and iPadOSSettings, Camera categoryYes, per appGreen dot
Pixel, Galaxy and other phonesSettings, privacy panelYes, plus "only while using"Green camera icon (version 12 and later)
WebsitesSite-info icon by the address barYes, per siteThe system indicator still shows

Then run through this access control checklist every few months:

  • Review every app with camera rights and revoke any you haven't opened in 30 days.
  • Choose "while using" over "always" wherever it's offered.
  • Remove site approvals for pages you visited only once.
  • On managed devices, expect your company's device policy to override your own switches.

faq.question: Why can't my app see my camera even after I granted permission?
faq.answer: Some apps cache permission states and need a full restart to recognise new settings. Close the app completely, reopen it, and check again. On Windows you may also need to restart the service or your PC after changing privacy settings.

faq.question: How do I turn on camera access in Windows 10 or 11?
faq.answer: Go to Start > Settings > Privacy & Security > Camera. Toggle 'Camera access' on at the top, then scroll down to find the specific app and enable it there too. Note that classic desktop apps (.exe) may not appear in this list — those apps access the camera directly through the driver.

faq.question: How do I allow camera access on iPhone or iPad (iOS)?
faq.answer: Open the Settings app, tap Privacy & Security, then tap Camera. You'll see a list of apps that have requested access — toggle on any app you want to allow. If an app isn't listed, it hasn't requested permission yet; try opening the app and triggering the camera feature first.

faq.question: How do I enable camera permissions on Android?
faq.answer: Go to Settings > Apps (or Application Manager), select the app in question, tap Permissions, and enable Camera. On newer Android versions you can also go to Settings > Privacy > Permission Manager > Camera to see all apps at once.

faq.question: How do I grant camera access in Google Chrome?
faq.answer: Click the lock icon (or camera icon) in the address bar while on the website that needs access. Select 'Allow' next to Camera and reload the page. You can also manage all site permissions via Chrome Settings > Privacy and Security > Site Settings > Camera.

faq.question: Why do desktop apps sometimes not appear in Windows camera settings?
faq.answer: Traditional Win32 desktop applications (such as older video conferencing software) communicate directly with camera drivers rather than going through the Windows privacy layer. This means they won't show up in Settings > Privacy & Security > Camera. You'll need to manage permissions within the app itself or update to a modern version.

faq.question: How do I revoke camera access for an app I no longer trust?
faq.answer: On Windows go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Camera and toggle off the specific app. On iOS go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Camera and toggle the app off. On Android go to Settings > Privacy > Permission Manager > Camera and select 'Deny' for the app.

faq.question: Can a website access my camera without asking permission?
faq.answer: No — all modern browsers require a site to explicitly request camera permission before accessing it, and the browser will display a prompt asking you to allow or block. If you previously clicked 'Allow', the site can access the camera on future visits without re-prompting. You can reset this by clearing the site's permissions in your browser settings.
